title: HLP Solutions Inc. CRA Expert Witness Order (2015 TCC)
subject: TCC interlocutory order on the admissibility and impartiality of a CRA employee testifying as an expert witness in an SR&ED trial.
summary: In HLP Solution Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 41), the Tax Court of Canada refused to qualify a CRA research and technology advisor as the Crown's expert witness in an SR&ED appeal. Because she had participated in every stage of the file, she lacked the impartiality required under Rule 145; CRA employment alone was not disqualifying.
metaDescription: Examine the February 2015 Tax Court of Canada order regarding a CRA expert witness in the HLP Solutions Inc. SR&ED tax case.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary and Background of the Case

On December 8, 2014, the Tax Court of Canada (TCC), sitting in Montréal under the general procedure in docket number 2012-671(IT)G, heard in a voir dire the challenge by HLP Solution Inc. to the qualification of the respondent's expert in the appeal brought by that company against the assessment issued by the Minister of National Revenue for the taxation year ending June 30, 2009, with Justice Johanne D'Auray subsequently delivering her decision orally, by teleconference from Ottawa, on January 12, 2015 (2015 TCC 41). The substantive dispute concerned the Minister's refusal, following the audit by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), to allow the tax credits claimed under the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program for part of Project 1 (mobile synchronization software) and for the whole of Project 2 (parallel mail collector). Since the CRA did not respond to its notice of objection, the appellant company appealed to the Court. The fundamental issue in this appeal lay both in the technical characterization of the computer work undertaken by the taxpayer and in the admissibility of the evidence put forward by the tax authorities to justify rejecting the claims.

At this hearing, the Crown sought to have Ms. Rosu, an active employee of the CRA holding a doctorate in computer science, recognized as an expert witness so that she could provide the Court with opinion evidence on the scientific and technological eligibility of the two software projects at issue. The taxpayer HLP Solution Inc. raised a formal objection to the qualification of this public servant as an expert witness; without contesting either her expertise or the fact that she had been employed by the CRA as a research and technology advisor (RTA) since February 2009, it argued that Ms. Rosu, who had written the technical review report on which the assessment was based, written an addendum confirming her initial position and attended all meetings with the appellant, lacked the impartiality required to objectively assist the Court on the decisive question of the eligibility of the work for SR&ED.

The legislative and regulatory framework governing this dispute rests on two complementary pillars of Canadian tax law. Substantively, the eligibility of software development work is governed by the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" set out in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act (ITA), which operates in tandem with the expenditure deduction mechanisms under section 37 and the investment tax credit calculations in subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA. More specifically, paragraph 248(1)(c) of the ITA covers experimental development, defined as all work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement in order to create new materials, devices, products or processes or to improve, even slightly, existing ones. Correlatively, paragraph 248(1)(d) includes in this definition work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing and psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs of, and directly in support of, basic research, applied research or experimental development undertaken in Canada. Conversely, paragraph 248(1)(i) expressly excludes from the statutory definition the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product, as well as the commercial use of a new or improved process.

Procedurally and evidentially, the admissibility of opinion evidence before the Tax Court of Canada is strictly governed by section 145 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) (SOR/90-688a) and by Form 145(2), entitled Certificate Concerning Code of Conduct for Expert Witnesses. These regulatory provisions impose on the expert witness the overriding duty to assist the Court impartially, objectively and independently on matters within the witness's area of expertise, this duty to the Court prevailing over any duty to the party that employs or has retained the witness.

In reasons delivered orally on January 12, 2015 (following the voir dire held on December 8, 2014), the transcript of which was signed on February 18, 2015, Justice Johanne D'Auray of the Tax Court of Canada allowed the objection raised by HLP Solution Inc. and refused to recognize Ms. Rosu as an expert witness on the ground that, because of her involvement at every stage of the file, she lacked the necessary impartiality, while expressly specifying that she was not disqualifying her because she was a CRA employee. At paragraphs [41] to [44] of her reasons delivered in French, the judge relied in particular on the recent TCC precedent in Les Abeilles Service de conditionnement inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313, docket number 2011-2054(IT)G, judgment rendered on October 23, 2014 by Justice Gaston Jorré), a decision in which the respondent's expert, who had written the technical review report underlying the assessment, was found not to be impartial, Justice Jorré giving his testimony very limited weight as expert evidence and accepting it only as factual evidence of his role at the audit stage, without having to formally rule on the objection. The order does not, however, cite the decision in Highland Foundry Ltd. v. The Queen (docket number 92-264, August 15, 1994); rather, it relies on R. v. Mohan (Supreme Court of Canada, 1994) and R. v. Abbey (Ontario Court of Appeal, 2009), as well as on Les Abeilles and Gagné v. The Queen (2002). Paragraphs [18] to [20] of Highland Foundry, for their part, highlighted the structural conflict between a CRA official's administrative obligation to apply the Agency's internal policies and a court expert's duty to formulate an opinion based on the first principles of his or her scientific discipline. Consequently, the TCC excluded Ms. Rosu's opinion evidence at the qualification stage and, since it had given the appellant time to complete its own expert's report, gave the respondent the opportunity to file a new expert report, the filing date to be agreed between the parties in light of the hearing dates scheduled for the end of April; the judge reiterated that an expert witness need not be independent but must be impartial, and ruled that costs would follow the cause.
2. Fundamental Legal, Procedural and Evidentiary Failures

Analysis of the order rendered in HLP Solution Inc. and of the related case law to which it refers reveals a twofold structural problem: on the one hand, a major procedural and institutional failure by the tax authorities in the presentation of scientific evidence before the courts and, on the other hand, the recurring technical, contractual and documentary vulnerabilities of taxpayers that trigger these SR&ED disputes.
2.1. The Crown's Evidentiary Failure: Lack of Impartiality and Confusion Between Administrative Policies and Legislative Standards

The Court's decision to exclude Ms. Rosu's expert testimony crystallizes a rule of evidence that is now unavoidable in Canadian tax litigation: a CRA employee who has participated in every stage of the file — notably by writing the technical review report on which the assessment was based — can hardly have the detachment needed to act as an impartial aid to justice, although the mere fact of being employed by the CRA does not in itself constitute a ground for disqualification. When an SR&ED dispute moves beyond the administrative stage of the local audit or the second review triggered by a notice of objection and is brought before the Tax Court of Canada, the nature of the evidentiary inquiry changes radically.

In the day-to-day performance of their claim assessment duties, the CRA's research and technology advisors (RTAs) and in-house scientists are subject to administrative directives, their teams' claims review manuals and the Agency's policy statements, such as the former Information Circular IC 86-4R3 or the consolidated policies that succeeded it. Yet, as the case law pointed out in Highland Foundry Ltd. (at paragraphs [18] to [20]) and in Les Abeilles Service de conditionnement inc. (2014 TCC 313), these administrative documents are not the law and frequently introduce restrictive definitions that depart from the general scheme of subsection 248(1) of the ITA.

To act as a truly impartial expert witness within the meaning of section 145 of the Tax Court of Canada Rules (General Procedure) and the Form 145(2) certificate, a CRA scientist who personally reviewed the claim at the audit stage is placed in a delicate position: as Justice D'Auray noted at paragraphs [33] and [34], it is very difficult for a person who has participated in every stage of a file to form a new opinion that disregards his or her previous opinions, Ms. Rosu having herself acknowledged that it is difficult to change one's opinion if the facts do not change. In Les Abeilles (paras. [88] to [91]), Justice Jorré added that such an expert must detach himself or herself from the administrative guidelines of his or her own employer and form his or her own opinion in order to assess the taxpayer's work according to his or her own expertise in the relevant profession or scientific discipline — in this case computer science and software engineering — as well as according to the ordinary meaning of the words of the statute. The classic illustration drawn from Highland Foundry demonstrates the extent of this dissonance: whereas the scientific community and ordinary dictionaries define a "prototype" according to its intrinsic nature as a first model for testing and conceptual validation, CRA administrative policy imposes on it a much narrower tax definition aimed at systematically excluding models capable of subsequent commercial exploitation. Similarly, in Les Abeilles Service de conditionnement inc., the Court noted (paras. [91] to [96]) that the Crown's expert witness, Mr. Kooi, often seemed guided more by CRA guidelines and policies — his report in fact concluding with a reference to SR&ED Application Policy 2002-02R2 — than by his own expertise, rather than delivering an independent scientific analysis. In invoking this precedent at paragraphs [41] to [44] of the HLP Solution Inc. order, however, the TCC based its own decision not on the application of CRA internal policies, but on Ms. Rosu's lack of detachment, revealed by her participation in every stage of the file, the word-for-word reproduction of passages from her technical review report, the use of "we" to refer to the CRA and the confusion between her role as RTA and that of expert witness (paras. [31] to [40]); the Court did not require the use of an external expert, but gave the Crown the opportunity to file a new expert report.
2.2. Substantive and Documentary Failures at the Heart of SR&ED Disputes in Software Engineering and Engineering

Although the order signed on February 18, 2015 (reasons delivered on January 12, 2015) decides, on a preliminary basis, the question of the admissibility of the expert evidence, the underlying dispute concerning HLP Solution Inc.'s two software development projects (mobile synchronization software and parallel mail collector) for the taxation year ending June 30, 2009 falls squarely within the analytical framework of the five case-law criteria for SR&ED eligibility. These five criteria, formulated by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd., approved by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. and summarized in C.W. Agencies Inc. (2001 FCA 393), are restated at paragraphs [141] to [143] of Les Abeilles Service de conditionnement inc. (2014 TCC 313) — a decision cited by the judge in HLP Solution Inc. solely on the question of the expert's impartiality — and require examining: first, whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures; second, whether the person formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty; third, whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses; fourth, whether the process resulted in a technological advancement; and fifth, whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results was kept as the work progressed. In the practice of disputes brought before the TCC, four major failures cause projects to be disqualified or fuel CRA challenges.
2.3. Confusion Surrounding Technological Uncertainty and the Definition of the State of Technology

The first cause of disputes in software development projects lies in the difficulty of establishing the existence of genuine technological uncertainty within the meaning of subsection 248(1) of the ITA. In Canadian tax law, technological uncertainty is a reality that exists in the mind of the competent professional when whether a given objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, cannot be determined or resolved on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge and ordinary experience. Taxpayers in the information technology sector frequently fail before the CRA when their claims describe functional business objectives, application programming interface integration difficulties or ordinary debugging problems that fall within routine engineering rather than a fundamental limitation of software architecture or algorithmics.

Conversely, the decision in Les Abeilles Service de conditionnement inc. — the HLP Solution Inc. order not ruling on the merits — highlights an error of assessment committed by the CRA's scientific advisor: the application of an excessively narrow view of the "state of technology," consisting notably of examining each test in isolation rather than the project as a whole (paras. [9], [135] and [153]). In Les Abeilles, where the projects sought increased efficiency achieved without excessive expenditure (para. [11]) and where the appellant had found no ready-made solution through its client's network, its suppliers or on the Web (paras. [49] to [51] and [155]), the appellant's expert explained in cross-examination (para. [137]) that carrying out a project at lower cost when the technology exists elsewhere at a higher cost may constitute an advancement; from this perspective, the need to develop a cost-effective solution may be relied on in support of technological uncertainty where existing solutions and knowledge are not commercially or practically viable in the taxpayer's operational context. When the taxpayer fails to document, from the outset of the project, how the solutions already available on the market were technically or economically impracticable for achieving the required performance objectives, the CRA systematically rejects the claim on the ground that the underlying technology already existed elsewhere in the world.
2.4. Failure to Demonstrate a Systematic Approach of Experimentation and Analysis

The second major failure concerns proof that the research was conducted in a field of science or technology "by means of experiment or analysis," in accordance with the explicit wording of subsection 248(1) of the ITA. In both software engineering and manufacturing engineering, businesses often proceed through rapid empirical adjustments or iterative development methodologies without formalizing the logical structure of their approach. If the taxpayer cannot demonstrate that its tests formed part of a methodical progression — in which each series of tests flows from a specific technical hypothesis aimed at overcoming an identified obstacle, such as the sequence of three successive solutions (manual, hybrid, then by a cylinder system) described at paragraph [55] of Les Abeilles — CRA auditors characterize the work as ordinary trial and error lacking a systematic character. It is precisely on this ground that the involvement of an independent expert witness on the taxpayer's side proves decisive before the TCC, because this expert can demonstrate to the judge how the technical facts of the file align rigorously with the five case-law criteria, including that of adherence to the scientific method.
2.5. Insufficiency and Mischaracterization of Contemporaneous Documentation

The question of contemporaneous documentation is the most frequent point of friction during SR&ED audits. In its Claims Review Manual for research and technology advisors, the CRA tends to treat the presence of formal contemporaneous documents as an almost absolute requirement. However, from a strictly legal standpoint, the Tax Court of Canada held at paragraph [94] of Les Abeilles Service de conditionnement inc. (relying, at footnote 41, on the principle set out by Judge Archambault in 116736 Canada Inc. v. Canada, [1998] T.C.J. No. 478 (QL)) that the existence of contemporaneous documents with specific predetermined content is not a legal precondition to SR&ED eligibility under the ITA, the Court further noting at paragraph [143] (and footnote 70) that the five case-law criteria are not absolute.

Nevertheless, the Court adds a fundamental evidentiary nuance: although contemporaneous documentation is not a substantive condition imposed by the statute, it often remains necessary in practice to establish the facts or to decide between conflicting versions before the Court. In software development projects similar to those of HLP Solution Inc., the evidentiary failure occurs when the business overwrites its intermediate code versions, keeps no record of rejected architectures and attempts to reconstruct its hypotheses several years after the fact during the audit. Likewise, when test decisions are made verbally at daily operational meetings — as the company's president explained at paragraph [30] of Les Abeilles — the taxpayer that does not keep at least a structured list of the work and tests carried out exposes itself to immediate administrative rejection and an extremely heavy burden of proof on appeal.
2.6. The Commercial Production Boundary, Test Materials and Contractual Exclusions

Finally, SR&ED disputes regularly involve the strict delineation between experimental development eligible under paragraphs 248(1)(c) and (d) of the ITA and the commercial activities excluded by paragraph 248(1)(i), as well as the treatment of inputs or funding provided by clients. At paragraphs [29] to [35] of Les Abeilles, the Court examines a complex industrial arrangement: the client (Mabe/General Electric) supplied free of charge the components used for the tests, retrieved the subassemblies after testing to send them to Mexico to be disassembled, then required progressive deliveries of parts during pilot runs in which the parts were incorporated into dryers sold on the market.

The survival of an SR&ED claim in such a context depends on the taxpayer's ability to draw a flawless accounting and legal dividing line. On the one hand, the Court specified at paragraph [35] of Les Abeilles that the stages following the testing phase — in particular the pilot runs whose parts are marketed — were not part of the dispute; out of prudence, these stages should be excluded from the claim in light of paragraph 248(1)(i) of the ITA. On the other hand, when software or manufacturing projects are carried out within a client-supplier relationship, the absence of contractual clauses clearly distinguishing the sale of a standard product from the performance of research services on behalf of a third party results in the receipts being characterized as "contract payments" within the meaning of subsection 127(9) of the ITA, which correspondingly reduces, under subsection 127(18) of the ITA, the eligible expenditures used to calculate the supplier's investment tax credits.
3. Comparative Summary Table of Legal and Evidentiary Requirements

The following table summarizes each legal, procedural and case-law requirement arising from the HLP Solution Inc. order, the leading decision to which it refers (Les Abeilles Service de conditionnement inc.) and Highland Foundry Ltd., setting out side by side the respective failures of the Crown and of taxpayers as well as the standard of proof applied by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Standard of Proof and the Court's Assessment Criterion

cells: Impartiality and independence of the expert witness
Section 145 and Form 145(2) of the TCC Rules (General Procedure); HLP Solution Inc. (2015 TCC 41), paras. [31]–[49]; Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313).

Crown failure: Presentation, as an expert witness, of a CRA employee (Ms. Rosu, D.Sc. in computer science) who had participated in every stage of the file (technical review report on which the assessment was based, addendum, meetings with the appellant), which deprived her of the necessary detachment, and not because of her employment relationship with the CRA alone.

Exclusion of the expert lacking impartiality: The expert witness need not be independent, but must be impartial; disqualification may be ordered at the qualification stage following a cost-benefit analysis (Mohan; Abbey). A CRA employee who participated in every stage of the file and defends the opinion formed at the audit does not have the impartiality required to advise the Court on SR&ED eligibility.
Primacy of scientific first principles over administrative policy
Subsection 248(1) ITA; Highland Foundry Ltd. (1994), paras. [18]–[20]; Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313), paras. [88]–[96] (the HLP Solution Inc. order, 2015 TCC 41, does not rule on this question).

Crown failure: Assessment of eligibility according to the restrictive definitions of CRA internal policies (such as the Agency's guidelines and Application Policy 2002-02R2 relied on in Les Abeilles, or the narrow tax definition of "prototype") rather than according to the statute and science.

Independent legal and scientific interpretation: The expert opinion must rest on the first principles of the scientific discipline concerned and the ordinary meaning of the words of the ITA, without being bound by CRA administrative directives.
Existence of genuine technological uncertainty
Paragraph 248(1)(c) ITA; Northwest Hydraulic, RIS-Christie and C.W. Agencies (2001 FCA 393); Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313), paras. [49]–[51], [141]–[143], [155].

Taxpayer and CRA failure: On the taxpayer's side, description of functional objectives without evidence of the limits of the art; on the CRA's side (Les Abeilles), examination of each test in isolation rather than the project as a whole and characterization of the work as standard engineering practice despite the absence of accessible ready-made solutions.

Proof of the insufficiency of accessible knowledge: Demonstration on a balance of probabilities that known solutions were non-existent or commercially and technically impracticable for achieving the targeted objectives.
Formulation of hypotheses and systematic experimentation
Preamble and paragraphs 248(1)(c) and (d) ITA; Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313), paras. [55]–[57], [157].
Taxpayer failure: Reliance on unstructured empirical debugging without any statement of causal hypotheses or demonstration of a logical series of experimental iterations.

Traceability of the scientific method: Proof of a systematic approach by means of experiment or analysis (observation, hypothesis, controlled testing, logical analysis of results) supported by an independent expert witness.
Keeping contemporaneous documents
Subsection 248(1) ITA; 116736 Canada Inc. ([1998] T.C.J. No. 478 (QL)); Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313), paras. [30], [94].
Taxpayer failure: Failure to archive unsuccessful tests and intermediate versions when test decisions are made at daily meetings, weakening the factual evidence.

Legal flexibility but evidentiary requirement: Contemporaneous documentation with pre-established content is not a legal precondition to eligibility, but probative exhibits (test lists, logs) and credible testimony are required to prove contested facts.
Delineation of commercial production and third-party inputs
Paragraphs 248(1)(d) and 248(1)(i) ITA; subsection 127(9) ITA; Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313), paras. [29]–[35].
Taxpayer failure: Confusion between experimental tests, commercial pilot runs and client-funded deliverables.

Strict segregation of phases and expenditures: Total exclusion of post-testing phases (pilot production sold on the market) and of materials supplied free of charge, limiting the claim to the claimant's own salaries and materials incurred during the experimental phase.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Case Studies and Corrective Compliance Measures

In order to translate the case-law lessons of the HLP Solution Inc. order and of Les Abeilles Service de conditionnement inc. into operational protocols that Canadian businesses can apply directly, the following two case studies set out in detail the restructuring of projects confronted with the exact pitfalls identified by the Tax Court of Canada.
4.1. Case Study No. 1: Software Development and Distributed Architectures (HLP Solution Inc. Model)
Industrial Context and Initial Legal Pitfalls

The Canadian company LogiFlux Analytique inc. designs high-frequency transaction processing software platforms. During its fiscal year, the company undertakes two major software development projects aimed at creating an engine for real-time reconciliation of heterogeneous data streams with a guaranteed latency of less than five milliseconds, and claims SR&ED investment tax credits in this regard covering the salaries of its software engineers. Following the audit, the CRA rejects both projects in their entirety.

This refusal stems from a series of structural failures. First, the technical descriptions submitted by the company emphasize the product's commercial features rather than the theoretical computer science barriers related to memory contention and lock-free serialization, leading the CRA auditor to conclude that the work was routine programming. Second, the development team works according to an agile methodology, systematically overwriting unsuccessful experimental branches in its source code manager (Git) so as to keep only the functional code delivered to production, thereby depriving itself of any contemporaneous material evidence of its iterations. Third, an institutional client paid a lump sum under a software services agreement drafted in general terms, which allows the CRA to characterize this payment as a contract payment within the meaning of subsection 127(9) of the ITA, reducing the eligible expenditures to nil under subsection 127(18) of the ITA. Fourth, when the file is appealed to the Tax Court of Canada, the Crown files the expert report of an in-house CRA computer scientist holding a doctorate, who assesses the projects against the restrictive administrative definitions in CRA manuals rather than according to the first principles of computer science.
Step 1: Restructuring Project Governance and Characterizing Technological Uncertainty According to First Principles

To overcome these objections and fully satisfy paragraphs 248(1)(c) and (d) of the ITA, LogiFlux Analytique inc. must first reform its project governance by formally separating the product's functional roadmap (intended for the market) from the computer science research protocol (intended to resolve technological uncertainties). Before undertaking any experimental coding, the director of software architecture writes a state-of-technology assessment memorandum documenting the preliminary tests carried out with the standard stream-processing engines available on the market. This document demonstrates, with profiling measurements in support, that standard garbage collection and thread locking mechanisms generate irreducible pauses of 45 milliseconds under the imposed load, rendering known solutions technically impracticable. By defining the obstacle not as a business objective but as a fundamental conflict between transactional consistency and non-blocking memory allocation according to the first principles of theoretical computer science, the company establishes the existence of indisputable technological uncertainty in the mind of a competent professional.
Step 2: Overhauling Contemporaneous Documentation and Systematic Tracking of Experimentation

Although the Tax Court of Canada confirmed at paragraph [94] of Les Abeilles that keeping contemporaneous documents in a pre-established format is not a legal precondition to eligibility, the ability to prove factually the application of the scientific method remains essential in the event of litigation. LogiFlux Analytique inc. therefore reconfigures its software engineering tools (Jira and Git) so that the documentary trail is generated organically as the work proceeds. The company formally prohibits the deletion or destructive merging (squash and merge) of experimental code branches. Each architectural attempt is isolated in a dedicated branch and associated with a digital experimentation record that must capture the algorithmic hypothesis formulated before coding, the parameters of the automated test bench, the raw test logs recording the measured results and the logical analysis explaining why the hypothesis was disproved or partially validated. In parallel, the time tracking system is segmented so as to charge to the SR&ED cost centre only the hours devoted to experimental branches and to programming and data collection work directly in support of and commensurate with the needs of these tests under paragraph 248(1)(d) of the ITA, while isolating in the accounts the coding of commercial interfaces excluded by paragraph 248(1)(i).
Step 3: Re-engineering Contractual Clauses to Prevent the Exclusion of Funded Research

To neutralize the risk of client revenues being recharacterized as contract payments within the meaning of subsection 127(9) of the ITA, the legal advisors of LogiFlux Analytique inc. carry out a complete overhaul of the commercial contracts concluded with users of the platform. The contractual wording is restructured to establish unambiguously that the subject matter of the agreement relates exclusively to the grant of a commercial licence to use a software product for a flat fee tied to compliance with a Service Level Agreement, without any contractual obligation to perform scientific research or experimental development on behalf of the customer. The intellectual property clauses stipulate that all source code, algorithms, mathematical models and technological knowledge developed remain the exclusive and absolute property of LogiFlux Analytique inc., with the client acquiring no rights in the underlying work. Finally, the contract specifies that the company alone bears the entire financial and technical risk if the optimization work fails and retains complete methodological autonomy over the conduct of its internal engineering.
Step 4: Procedural Strategy and Management of Expert Evidence Before the Tax Court of Canada

Should the CRA maintain its refusal and the appeal proceed before the Tax Court of Canada, LogiFlux Analytique inc. deploys an evidentiary strategy directly aligned with the HLP Solution Inc. order and section 145 of the TCC Rules (General Procedure). On the offensive side, the company retains an independent university professor specializing in distributed computer systems, dealing at arm's length with the company, to sign the Certificate Concerning Code of Conduct for Expert Witnesses (Form 145(2)) and produce an expert report mapping the archived code branches against the five eligibility criteria in the case law. On the defensive side, if the Crown attempts to present as an expert witness a CRA employee who participated in the audit of the file, counsel for the taxpayer raise a formal objection in a voir dire based on paragraphs [31] to [49] of the HLP Solution Inc. order, on Les Abeilles (2014 TCC 313) and on paragraphs [18] to [20] of the Highland Foundry decision (1994). This objection seeks to demonstrate that this official, because of his or her participation in the earlier stages of the file and the confusion between his or her role as RTA and that of expert (for example, the verbatim reuse of his or her technical review report), does not have the impartiality required to assist the Court, which may lead to the exclusion of his or her opinion evidence; the mere fact of being employed by the CRA would not, however, suffice to justify that exclusion.
4.2. Case Study No. 2: Industrial Automation and Shop Floor Process Engineering (Les Abeilles Service de conditionnement inc. Model)
Industrial Context and Initial Legal Pitfalls

The manufacturing company MécaPrécision Assemblage inc., located in Montréal, manufactures and assembles electromechanical subassemblies — notably heating elements and control panels — for a large multinational original equipment manufacturer in the household appliance sector. In order to prevent production from being relocated to Mexico and to ensure innovative manufacturing in Canada, the company undertakes to design in-house an automated assembly and testing line capable of producing 174 panel variations from 600 possible components within a maximum of four hours after the order, while resolving a critical problem of "false rejects" occurring at the high-speed test stations.

The company claims approximately $400,000 in technician and engineer salaries and $5,000 in materials for SR&ED. The CRA denies the claim on three main grounds: first, industrial automation systems allegedly already existed on the international market, so that the search for a cost-effective or plant-specific solution would not constitute a technological advancement according to the narrow view of the state of technology adopted by the auditor; second, the shop floor tests were decided verbally at daily operational meetings without written laboratory protocols, which would allegedly invalidate the systematic character of the research; third, the multinational client supplied the tested components free of charge and subsequently incorporated batches of parts into appliances sold on the market during pilot runs, leading the CRA to conclude that there was commercial production excluded by paragraph 248(1)(i) of the ITA.
Step 1: Characterizing Technological Uncertainty Based on the Impracticability of Existing Solutions and Physical Constraints

Relying directly on the doctrine established by the TCC in Les Abeilles Service de conditionnement inc. (2014 TCC 313) — a decision on which the HLP Solution Inc. order relies — MécaPrécision Assemblage inc. restructures the demonstration of its technological uncertainty around two complementary axes. On the techno-economic front, engineering management assembles an initial documentary file establishing that it searched for solutions already available on the market at the start of the project, but that existing commercial robotic lines were either technically incapable of handling the combinatorics of 174 variations on a single line within a four-hour window, or financially impracticable given the economic parameters of North American subcontracting. In Les Abeilles, the TCC found that there was technological uncertainty because the appellant did not know at the outset how to achieve its objectives and had found no ready-made solution (paras. [154] to [156] and [166]), the appellant's expert having also indicated that carrying out a project at lower cost than with a more expensive existing technology may constitute an advancement (para. [137]). On the mechanical physics front, the file precisely characterizes the dynamics of the false-reject problem at the test station: the mechanical shock wave generated by the impact between the rapidly moving heating element and the stop designed to hold it at the test station produces a shock that displaces the element and distorts the test (as the Court found at paragraph [56] of Les Abeilles), creating a kinematic and vibratory uncertainty that routine engineering cannot resolve without degrading cycle time.
Step 2: Structuring Shop Floor Experimental Tracking and Recording Iterations

To reconcile the operational reality of a plant where test decisions are made at daily morning meetings with the TCC's evidentiary requirements, MécaPrécision Assemblage inc. implements a chronological log of work and tests directly inspired by the test log referred to in footnote 1 of the judgment, at paragraphs [30] and [36] (footnote 12) and in Appendix A of Les Abeilles. Without imposing bureaucratic burdens incompatible with shop floor work, each daily operational meeting gives rise to a dated entry in a structured technical tracking table. This log traces the logical lineage of the hypotheses tested across each series of prototypes: for example, for the problem of proximity between the heating element and the housing, it documents the move from a first manual solution requiring a special tool, to a second hybrid solution incorporating a thumb detector, to a third solution using a cylinder system, while for the test station it records the installation of a linear-motion stop that no longer causes a shock capable of displacing the element. Likewise, for the panel assembly line, the log documents the experimentation with the ergonomic and logistical approach in which an attendant gathers the required components from among the 600 part numbers and brings them to the assembler, who carries out the work without moving, much like a surgeon receiving instruments. By recording for each test the parameters modified, the number of parts tested, the false-reject rate observed and the exact hours devoted by the technicians, the company has a key exhibit (comparable to Tab 5 of Exhibit A-1 in Les Abeilles) making it possible to establish, on a balance of probabilities, the systematic character of the experimental development within the meaning of paragraph 248(1)(c) of the ITA.
Step 3: Contractual Ring-Fencing of Loaned Components and a Strict Cut-Off Before the Commercial Pilot Run

To guard against any challenge based on the commercial production exclusion in paragraph 248(1)(i) of the ITA or on client funding, MécaPrécision Assemblage inc. formalizes in writing with its multinational original equipment manufacturer the protocol governing test inputs and approval phases, modelling it on the factual structure described at paragraphs [29] to [35] of Les Abeilles. The agreement stipulates that the components supplied free of charge by the client for the tests remain the client's property and are neither invoiced nor claimed for tax purposes by MécaPrécision; once the shop floor tests are completed, the subassemblies assembled during the tests are returned to the client, which ships them to its facilities in Mexico to be disassembled, thereby demonstrating the complete absence of commercialization of the test batches. Only the materials acquired directly by MécaPrécision to modify its test benches (like the approximately $1,300 in materials claimed for project 2007-01 in Les Abeilles) and the direct salaries of its employees assigned to the tests are included in the SR&ED claim. In addition, accounting governance requires an immediate and final halt to SR&ED time recording as soon as the technical validation phase ends: all subsequent stages in which the company supplies increasing volumes of parts to the client for production approval, including the pilot run during which the parts are incorporated into dryers sold on the market, are entirely excluded from the tax claim.
Step 4: Retaining an External Mechanical Engineering Expert Witness and Neutralizing the CRA's Expert

To complete its compliance and strengthen its file in view of possible judicial scrutiny, MécaPrécision Assemblage inc. retains an external scientific expert entirely independent of the company and of the CRA — such as an engineer holding a bachelor's degree in pure mathematics, a master's degree in aerospace engineering and a doctorate in mechanical engineering who has taught certain courses at École Polytechnique de Montréal, like the appellant's expert, Mr. Martin Gariépy, whose qualifications are described at paragraph [79] and who was recognized as an expert at paragraph [80] of Les Abeilles. This independent expert examines the shop floor facilities and the log of work and tests, then writes a report in compliance with section 145 of the TCC Rules (General Procedure) demonstrating how each series of tests meets the five case-law eligibility criteria according to the first principles of mechanical engineering. If the CRA persists in contesting the claim before the TCC by presenting as an expert witness one of its own employees who participated in the audit of the file, counsel for MécaPrécision immediately invoke the HLP Solution Inc. order (February 2015) and Les Abeilles (October 2014) to have this partial expertise excluded or, at the very least, its probative value reduced (Justice Jorré having given very little weight to the CRA's expert testimony in Les Abeilles, while Justice D'Auray excluded it at the qualification stage in HLP) and to secure the evidentiary preponderance of their independent expert.
4.3. Comparative Summary of the Corrective Measures Applied in the Case Studies

The table below summarizes the operational architecture of the remedial measures deployed in the two case studies in order to meet the requirements of the Income Tax Act and of the Tax Court of Canada.

body.text: 5. Strategic Conclusions and Case-Law Outlook

The Tax Court of Canada's order in HLP Solution Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC 41; reasons delivered orally on January 12, 2015 and signed on February 18, 2015), read in light of Les Abeilles Service de conditionnement inc. v. The Queen (2014 TCC 313) and Highland Foundry Ltd. v. The Queen (1994), marks a decisive turning point in the balance of procedural power in disputes relating to SR&ED tax credits in Canada. By refusing to grant a highly qualified CRA employee the status of expert witness because of her lack of impartiality — arising from her participation in every stage of the file, and not from her employment relationship alone, the Court having emphasized that an expert need not be independent — the Court draws a clear line between the administrative function of tax auditing exercised in a file and the judicial function of scientific expertise in that same file.

This case law has three major consequences for the practice of tax law and the management of SR&ED claims in Canada. First, through Les Abeilles — the HLP Solution Inc. order not itself ruling on the scope of administrative policies — it enshrines the primacy of the legislative text of subsection 248(1) of the ITA and of scientific first principles over the CRA's internal administrative directives. The Agency's auditors and policy writers cannot impose on the courts reductive administrative definitions — whether the notion of prototype, a truncated view of the state of technology that ignores the economic viability of solutions, or the formalistic requirement of pre-formatted contemporaneous documents — that unduly restrict the scope of the tax incentive intended by Parliament. Second, the HLP Solution Inc. order in practice obliges the Crown, when it intends to contest the scientific validity of a project before the TCC, to avoid presenting as an expert the advisor who conducted the audit and to use an impartial expert who was not involved in the earlier stages of the file, whether or not that expert is a CRA employee, which considerably raises the rigour of the adversarial debate and promotes a more objective resolution of files even before trial. Finally, this evolution in the case law reminds Canadian businesses that the key to success before the Tax Court of Canada lies in the combination of genuine traceability of tests — even when adapted to the agile realities of software or to daily shop floor meetings — strict segregation of commercial phases and the proactive use of an independent external expert witness capable of translating the technological complexity of the project into the analytical framework of the five criteria recognized by Canadian courts.

outcome: Order refusing to qualify the CRA advisor as an expert witness because she had worked on every stage of the file.
